questions.question: Relation R on the set of integers: aRb iff a² = b². Check reflexive, symmetric, transitive.
questions.solutionApproach: Reflexive: a²=a² always true → yes. Symmetric: a²=b² ⟹ b²=a² → yes. Transitive: a²=b² and b²=c² ⟹ a²=c² → yes. So R is an equivalence relation.
questions.answer: Reflexive, Symmetric, Transitive — R is an equivalence relation.

questions.question: R on positive integers: aRb iff a is a multiple of b (a = kb for some positive integer k). Is R a partial order?
questions.solutionApproach: Reflexive: a=1·a, yes. Antisymmetric: a=kb and b=ma ⟹ km=1 ⟹ k=m=1 ⟹ a=b, yes. Transitive: a=kb, b=mc ⟹ a=(km)c, yes. All three hold → Partial Order. Not total order since e.g. 2 and 3 are incomparable.
questions.answer: Yes, R is a Partial Order (but not a Total Order).

questions.question: How many reflexive AND symmetric relations exist on a 3-element set?
questions.solutionApproach: 3 diagonal pairs forced 'in' (reflexive). Off-diagonal pairs come in 3 mirror pairs: (1,2)/(2,1), (1,3)/(3,1), (2,3)/(3,2) — each mirror pair must be both-in or both-out together (symmetric) → 3 independent binary choices → 2^3 = 8.

questions.question: R and S are equivalence relations on A={1,2,3} where R groups {1,2} and {3}, and S groups {1} and {2,3}. Is R∪S an equivalence relation?
questions.solutionApproach: R∪S contains (1,2) [from R] and (2,3) [from S], so transitivity would require (1,3) ∈ R∪S. But neither R nor S relates 1 and 3. So transitivity fails.
questions.answer: No — R∪S is not an equivalence relation (fails transitivity).
